ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: ‘One thing’ leaves its object deliberately unspecified. Chan speakers ask whether such a thing exists, deny possessing one, challenge an interlocutor to name it, or make the phrase the grammatical subject of a open-ended statement.
EvidenceBody: Its Chan deployment includes positive, negative, indefinite, and deliberately unnamed forms. In the Nanyue-Huineng encounter, Nanyue says that "to describe it as one thing would not hit it" (說似一物即不中), after eight years of inquiry. Huineng's verse says, "awakening originally has no tree; the bright mirror is not a stand; originally there is not one thing; where could dust alight?" (菩提本無樹，明鏡亦非臺，本來無一物，何處惹塵埃). A lamp question quotes, "the hundred bones all collapse and scatter; one thing remains constantly numinous—what is the one thing?" and receives "what suffering, buddha!" (百骸俱潰散，一物鎮長靈；如何是一物；苦哉佛陀耶). Another address says, "outside, not one thing can establish [anything]; all are the original mind producing ten thousand kinds of things" (外無一物而能建立，皆是本心生萬種法). Later speakers also challenge anyone "not relying on one thing" (不依倚一物). These records use the ordinary noun precisely: sometimes an unnamed referent is proposed, sometimes even that label is rejected, and sometimes the phrase negates every external thing.
